statement.p: Sage can automate these computations for us. Before we begin, however, it will be helpful to understand how we can combine things using a list in Python. For instance, if the vectors v1, v2, and v3 form a basis for a subspace, we can bundle them together using square brackets: [v1, v2, v3]. Furthermore, we could assign this to a variable, such as basis = [v1, v2, v3].

Evaluating the following cell will load in some special commands.
sage.repl.load.load("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/davidaustinm/ula_modules/master/orthogonality.py", globals())
There is a command to apply the projection formula: projection(b, basis) returns the orthogonal projection of b onto the subspace spanned by basis, which is a list of vectors.
The command unit(w) returns a unit vector parallel to w.
Given a collection of vectors, say, v1 and v2, we can form the matrix whose columns are v1 and v2 using matrix([v1, v2]).T. When given a list of vectors, Sage constructs a matrix whose rows are the given vectors. For this reason, we need to apply the transpose.

Let's now consider W, the subspace of \real^5 having basis
\vvec_1 = \fivevec{14}{-6}{8}2{-6},\hspace{24pt} \vvec_2 = \fivevec{5}{-3}{4}3{-7},\hspace{24pt} \vvec_3 = \fivevec{2}30{-2}1.
Apply the Gram-Schmidt algorithm to find an orthogonal basis \wvec_1, \wvec_2, and \wvec_3 for W.
Find \bhat, the orthogonal projection of \bvec = \fivevec{-5}{11}0{-1}5 onto W.
Explain why we know that \bhat is a linear combination of the original vectors \vvec_1, \vvec_2, and \vvec_3 and then find weights so that
\bhat = c_1\vvec_1 + c_2\vvec_2 + c_3\vvec_3.
Find an orthonormal basis \uvec_1, \uvec_2, for \uvec_3 for W and form the matrix Q whose columns are these vectors.
Find the product Q^TQ and explain the result.
Find the matrix P that projects vectors orthogonally onto W and verify that P\bvec gives \bhat, the orthogonal projection that you found earlier.

li.p: We know that \bhat is in W and \vvec_1, \vvec_2, and \vvec_3 is a basis for W. We find \bhat=-\frac34\vvec_1+\frac12\vvec_2+2\vvec_3.
Q^TQ=I since the matrix product computes the dot products of the columns of Q.
